The body shows one history of harm; the political account shows how a community organised relationship; the royal book shows how conquest became obligation.

summary: The manuscript advances a coherent and valuable thesis: aggression cannot be ranked across societies as a single substance, and historical records reveal different layers of injury, coercion, organisation, and authority. Its strongest work closely reads the form of evidence—bones, monuments, legal cases, administrative protocols, letters, and broadcasts—and shows how institutions can organise harm or restraint. The chronological progression is intelligible, but adjacent chapters sometimes repeat cases and arguments, most conspicuously the overlapping Mongol material in Chapters 6 and 7. Nearly every section reiterates what the source does and does not establish, often through symmetrical caveats and open-ended questions; this produces rigor but also severe redundancy and a recognisably templated cadence. A substantial compression pass, sharper differentiation of chapter functions, and more sustained human narrative would make the book considerably more engaging without weakening its caution.
